The Declaration
and Address

Washington, Pennsylvania · 1809
Title up. → “Last week we ended on one sentence: the church of Christ upon earth is essentially, intentionally, and constitutionally one. Today: why anyone would need to write it.” Then the Design of Religion. The hour: Design 4 · Evils and proposition 10 6 · Christendom 10 · the sword 2 · Preamble 3 · conscience 6 · the solution 3 · Propositions 10 · our table 8 · reception and proof-sheets 5.
The Address

The Design of Religion

Start here. The Address is the long part, to “all that love our Lord Jesus Christ, in sincerity, throughout all the Churches.” Its first paragraph is the premise under everything that follows.
The Design of Religion

“That it is the grand design and native tendency of our holy religion to reconcile and unite men to God, and to each other, in truth and love, to the glory of God, and their own present and eternal good…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Stop before “will not, we presume, be denied.” Stand one, asked lightly: is unity what Christianity is for? If yes, every century of division is the religion failing its own purpose.
• “In truth and love”: both sides, from the first sentence. The motto later is “Union in Truth.”
The Design of Religion

“The nativity of its Divine author was announced from heaven, by a host of angels, with high acclamations of ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace and good-will toward men.’”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Same paragraph. The proof he offers is Luke 2: the religion was announced as peace.
The Design of Religion

“In so far, then, as this holy unity and unanimity in faith and love is attained, just in the same degree is the glory of God and the happiness of men promoted and secured.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• “Just in the same degree.” Unity is not a bonus on top of the religion; it is the measure of it. Then: what does division cost?
The Address

The Evils of Division

What division costs. Practical, not doctrinal. Build the list one line at a time and let the room map each one onto now.
“What awful and distressing effects have those sad divisions produced!”
“congregations broken to pieces”
“large settlements and tracts of country… entirely destitute of a Gospel ministry”
“How seldom do many… enjoy the dispensations of the Lord’s Supper, that great ordinance of unity and love”
“the tone of discipline relaxed… lest their people should leave them, and… find refuge in the bosom of another party”
“the weak stumbled, the graceless and profane hardened, the mouths of infidels opened to blaspheme religion”
Declaration and Address, 1809
Five clicks. All verbatim from the Evils of Division. The Supper line ties to the Table arc of the whole class. The last two land hardest in 2026: members who can leave for the church down the road, and the mouths of infidels. (Dropped from the list: “Several… who live at the door of a preached Gospel, dare not in conscience go to hear it”: people within reach of preaching, but of another party, whose scruples keep them from it, so they are as cut off as if among heathens. Restore if useful.)
The Evils of Division

“Say, dear brethren, are not these things so?”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• His own question, to the room. Let them answer.

Proposition 10

“Division among the Christians is a horrid evil, fraught with many evils.”

“It is antichristian, as it destroys the visible unity of the body of Christ; as if he were divided against himself…”
“It is antiscriptural, as being strictly prohibited by his sovereign authority…”
“It is antinatural, as it excites Christians to contemn, to hate, and oppose one another, who are bound… to love each other as brethren…”
Declaration and Address, 1809
Three clicks, verbatim. The Evils list was what division costs; this is what division is. Against Christ, against Scripture, against nature: a body excommunicating part of itself. Elided from the first: “excluding and excommunicating a part of himself.” From the second: “a direct violation of his express command.” Last clause: “In a word, it is productive of confusion and of every evil work.”
→ Then: it was not for want of trying. Here is fifteen hundred years of trying.

Christendom’s Search for Unity

Card. Lands after the Preamble’s despair (“amid the diversity and rancor of party contentions”) and before “anywhere but in Christ.” One click per slide. Eight to ten minutes with every slide; 1690 and 1799 are marked cuttable in their notes.

325 · Council of Nicaea

Arians against non-Arians. A creed, and fifty-six more years of war.
Constantine had just reunited the empire (324) and found the church at war over whether the Son is God. He convened the council himself, 325. The creed condemned Arius with the word homoousios.
' 'Failure: Constantine was baptized on his deathbed (337) by Eusebius of Nicomedia, an Arian sympathizer; his son Constantius pushed the empire Arian; Athanasius exiled five times; Jerome c. 360: “the whole world groaned and found itself Arian.” The creed people say today is the rewrite of 381. Goths, Vandals and Lombards stayed Arian into the 500s and 600s, then converted.
' '→ Say: the first creed written to unite the church did not unite the two sides; it named them.',

431 · Council of Ephesus

Does Mary bear God? A canon forbidding new creeds, and the Church of the East gone.
Nestorius of Constantinople objected to Theotokos; Cyril of Alexandria pressed the council. Cyril’s council opened before John of Antioch arrived; John’s party held its own council and each deposed the other’s leader; Theodosius II arrested both Cyril and Nestorius. A Formula of Reunion patched it in 433.
' 'Canon 7 of Ephesus: unlawful “to bring forward, or to write, or to compose a different faith as a rival to that established by the holy Fathers assembled with the Holy Ghost in Nicaea.” This is the ban the next council breaks, and the ban the East cites against the West in 1054.
' 'The Church of the East (Persia, outside the empire) had adopted Nicaea on its own at Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410; it refused Ephesus and has been separate ever since. Today: the Assyrian Church of the East.
' '→ Plant the canon. “We will come back to that.”',

451 · Council of Chalcedon

One nature or two? A Definition, “not a new creed,” and Egypt gone.
Chalcedon reaffirmed Ephesus’s ban on new creeds, then issued the Definition (“in two natures”) and said it was a definition, not a creed. The 381 creed is first read into the record here. Egypt, Armenia, Ethiopia, the Syriac churches refused it: the Oriental Orthodox, non-Chalcedonian to this day (Copts, Armenians, Ethiopians, Eritreans, Syriacs, Malankara).
' '→ The rhyme to plant: “not a new creed.” The thirteen propositions will say the same words.',

482 · The Henotikon

Zeno needs Egypt back. An “instrument of union,” and thirty-five years of schism with Rome.
Zeno’s Henotikon (482), drafted with Patriarch Acacius, tried to reconcile Chalcedonians and non-Chalcedonians by affirming Nicaea, Ephesus and Cyril and passing over Chalcedon in silence. Pope Felix III excommunicated Acacius (484). Rome and Constantinople were out of communion until 519 (Emperor Justin, the Formula of Hormisdas). It did not win Egypt back either.
' 'Later imperial compromises did the same thing twice more: 553 (Three Chapters, split the West for 150 years), 638 (Monothelitism, condemned in 680). Not on slides; say it in a sentence if you want the pattern.
' '→ A document literally named “instrument of union” produced the first schism between Rome and Constantinople.',

1054 · The Filioque

One word added to the creed. Legates sent to settle it, and East and West apart.
The Filioque (“and the Son”) entered the creed in Spain (Toledo 589), spread through the Frankish church, and was adopted at Rome about 1014. The East objected to the content and to the unilateral change, citing Ephesus Canon 7. Cardinal Humbert’s legation (1054) also contested leavened bread and papal primacy; on 16 July he laid the bull on the altar; Patriarch Cerularius anathematized the legates. The date is conventional; the estrangement was long and the 1204 sack sealed it. Mutual anathemas lifted 1965, communion not restored.
' '→ How do two churches with the same creed divide over the creed? Which version, and who decides.',

1530 · The Augsburg Confession

Luther’s protest. A confession offered as the basis for peace, and the West in two.
1517 the theses; 1521 Worms. The Augsburg Confession (25 June 1530, Melanchthon) was presented to Charles V at an imperial diet called to restore religious unity against the Turkish threat; its first articles affirm Nicaea. The Catholic theologians’ Confutation (3 August) rejected it; Charles gave the Protestants until April 1531 to submit. Trent (1545–63) anathematized the Protestant positions.
' '→ Shared creed, shared filioque, divided anyway. The creed was never the thing holding them together.',

1527 · Zurich

No creed this time. The magistrate. A council ruling, the sword, and Felix Manz drowned.
The exception that proves the rule: the other slides are a creed or a council offered for unity; this one is unity by force. The disputations of January and November 1525 were called to settle the quarrel, but what followed was a civic ruling and the river, not a creed. Connect it forward to the Preamble (“no man can judge for his brother”) and to the 1806 slide, where the Seceders split over whether the magistrate may enforce religion: unity by creed fails; unity by force fails worse.
Disputations January and November 1525; the council ordered infants baptized and rebaptizers banished, then (March 1526) drowned. Felix Manz drowned 5 January 1527, the first Protestant executed by Protestants. Schleitheim (February 1527, Michael Sattler) set out seven articles including believer’s baptism and separation from the sword; Sattler burned at Rottenburg that May. Zwingli wrote against Schleitheim the same year.
' 'Out of order by three years with Augsburg on purpose: Augsburg is the Catholic/Protestant split, this is the first split inside Protestantism.
' '→ The first Protestant unity ruling was enforced with the river.',

1529 · The Marburg Colloquy

The Lord’s Supper. Fourteen articles agreed, and “you have a different spirit.”
Marburg Colloquy, 1–4 October 1529, called by Philip of Hesse to unite the Protestants politically and theologically. The Marburg Articles: agreement on fourteen, and on the fifteenth (the Supper) agreement on everything except whether Christ’s body is bodily present. Luther’s line to the Swiss: “Ihr habt einen andern Geist.” Lutheran and Reformed have been separate confessional families since. The Formula of Concord (1577) settled Lutheran infighting by excluding the Reformed.
' '→ Thomas Campbell will call the Supper “that great ordinance of unity and love.” It is the one thing they could not agree on.',

1646 · The Westminster Confession

Three kingdoms at war. One confession for all three, and two thousand ministers ejected.
Solemn League and Covenant (1643): Scotland’s price for joining Parliament’s war was a common Presbyterian settlement for all three kingdoms. The Westminster Assembly (1643–49) produced the Confession (1646) and catechisms. The Independents (the “Dissenting Brethren”) argued against Presbyterian government inside the Assembly. Parliament never fully established it in England; the Restoration (1660) restored bishops; the Act of Uniformity (1662) ejected about two thousand ministers, the Great Ejection. Scotland adopted the Confession in 1647 and keeps it.
' '→ The confession Thomas Campbell was tried under was written to unite three kingdoms. It produced nonconformity.',

1690 · The Revolution Settlement

Scotland after the Revolution. Presbytery restored, and the Covenanters outside.
William and Mary’s settlement (1690) abolished bishops and established Presbyterianism with the Westminster Confession, but without the Covenants, which the state did not renew. The Cameronians (Society People) refused to enter and became the Reformed Presbyterian Church (1743 as a presbytery). The Episcopalians went out the other side.
' 'Cuttable: the Secession slide carries the Scottish story on its own.',

1733 · The Secession

Patrons appoint ministers. Erskine rebuked, and four ministers walk out.
The Patronage Act (1712) restored lay patrons’ right to present ministers. Erskine’s synod sermon (October 1732) attacked it; the Assembly rebuked him (1733); he and three others (Wilson, Moncrieff, Fisher) protested, were suspended, and formed the Associate Presbytery (December 1733). Deposed 1740. The Seceders renewed the Covenants; the Week 2 litany note has this.
' '→ His tradition began as a protest against imposed authority.',

1747 · The Burgess Oath

May a Seceder swear it? A synod vote, and mutual excommunication.
The oath, required of burgesses in Edinburgh, Glasgow and Perth: “the true religion presently professed within this realm and authorized by the laws thereof.” Burghers: it means only “not Catholic.” Anti-Burghers: it blesses the church we left. The synod split April 1747 (Associate Synod vs General Associate Synod); the Anti-Burghers excommunicated the Burghers (1748–49), and the two could not take communion together. Thomas Campbell was Anti-Burgher. The Week 2 litany note covers why it felt so large (the Testimony, the Covenants).
' '→ This is the rule Conemaugh broke, and the room already knows it.',

1799 · 1806 · Old Light, New Light

May the magistrate enforce religion? Revised Testimonies, and each synod in two.
The Burghers split 1799 (Original Burghers, Old Light), the Anti-Burghers 1806 (Constitutional Associate Presbytery, Old Light) over whether the civil magistrate has power in religion (Westminster Confession ch. 23). Campbell sided with the Old Lights by friendship more than conviction (Foster; Week 2 note). He sailed April 1807.
' 'Cuttable: the Week 2 litany already told this. Keep if the room needs the landing.',

…and today

Too many divisions to count.
The egg, shattered. Dozens of pieces, many of them named, the names chosen to make the room smile (four kinds of Church of Christ are in there). No click; it is simply on screen.
→ Every one of these was somebody’s instrument of unity.
The tree of divisions
Every branch is a church leaving another, placed at its year; time runs left to right, with the Reformation given most of the width. The leaves at the right edge are churches that still exist. Simplified and partial on purpose: the real tree does not fit on a wall.
→ Not one of these produced unity. Not one held even the people who signed it.
What every one of them had in common

Every one had a sword behind it.

Constantine · Theodosius · Marcian · Zeno · the papal legates
Charles V · the council of Zurich · Philip of Hesse · Parliament · William and Mary
the patrons · the burgess oath · the magistrate
Three clicks, back across the egg: who stood behind each instrument. Emperors convened Nicaea (Constantine), Ephesus (Theodosius II) and Chalcedon (Marcian), and issued the Henotikon (Zeno); legates carried Rome’s bull in 1054; Charles V received Augsburg; Zurich’s council ruled and drowned; Philip of Hesse called Marburg; Parliament imposed Westminster; the crown settled 1690; Parliament’s Patronage Act made the Secession; a civic oath made the Burgher split; and the last split was over whether the magistrate may enforce religion at all.
→ Every instrument of unity on that egg could be enforced. Not one held even the people who signed it.
The Address · why 1809, why here

“What dreary effects of those accursed divisions are to be seen, even in this highly favored country, where the sword of the civil magistrate has not as yet learned to serve at the altar.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• From the Evils of Division paragraph, just before “congregations broken to pieces.” The Address says it outright later: “A country happily exempted from the baneful influence of a civil establishment of any peculiar form of Christianity.”
• The First Amendment was eighteen years old; Pennsylvania had never had an established church. For the first time in the story, nobody could enforce a creed. So unity could not be imposed here. It would have to be found.
• → A few decades after one Declaration of Independence, another. Then: the people of the grove, and what they wanted.
The Declaration

Preamble

The sentiments of the people of the grove.
Summer 1809. The people following Thomas Campbell from farmhouse to maple grove have become something, and they need to say what. The Declaration is the short part, written for them. After the egg: this is what the people of the grove wanted, and why they despaired of getting it the old way.
Preamble

“…tired and sick of the bitter jarrings and janglings of a party spirit, we would desire to be at rest; and, were it possible, we would also desire to adopt and recommend such measures as would give rest to our brethren throughout all the churches…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The line everyone remembers. Say it slowly. “Rest” is the word they chose, not “victory.”
Preamble

“This desirable rest, however, we utterly despair either to find for ourselves, or to be able to recommend to our brethren, by continuing amid the diversity and rancor of party contentions, the veering uncertainty and clashings of human opinions…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Stop here. Do not read the next clause yet.
• → Before the answer, name the issue underneath all of it. Why can none of those instruments work?

Why did every instrument fail?

Card. Fifteen hundred years of creeds, councils and swords, and a document that despairs of the old way. The next slide names the reason underneath.
Anton von Werner, Luther at the Diet of Worms, 1877 · public domain
Worms, 1521

Conscience cannot be compelled.

Worms, April 1521. Asked to recant, Luther: “my conscience is captive to the Word of God. I cannot and will not recant anything, since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience.” (“Here I stand, I can do no other” is the famous form; the earliest printed accounts add it, the transcript does not. Say “as the story goes.”) Protestantism begins with that sentence, and it is the reason none of the instruments on the egg could work: a creed can name who agrees, and a sword can make people say it, but neither can make anyone believe. The consequence comes a few slides on.
Worms, 18 April 1521

“Unless I am convinced by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason (for I do not trust either in the pope or in councils alone, since it is well known that they have often erred and contradicted themselves), I am bound by the Scriptures I have quoted and my conscience is captive to the Word of God.”

Martin Luther at Worms, 18 April 1521
• The sentence the famous line ends. Look at how it starts: “Unless I am convinced.” He holds his own reading open. Show him from Scripture or clear reason that he is wrong, and he must change. That is the opposite of “I can do what I want.”
• Translations vary (“testimonies of the Holy Scriptures or evident reason”); this is the common English form.
• It ends with the line everyone remembers: “I cannot and will not recant anything, since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience.” (“Here I stand, I can do no other” is the later printed form.)

Conscience is not “I can do what I want.”

It is “I must.”
One click. His word is captive: bound, not free. Conscience here is not a preference but an obligation before God. “Neither safe nor right to go against conscience”: not safe, because he must answer to God for it.

Captive to the Word of God.

Not to the pope’s reading of it.
Not to a council’s.
Not even to his own.
Not to what he thinks it says. To what it says.
Four clicks; slow down on the third. The proof is the first clause of the sentence: “Unless I am convinced by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason.” He can still be corrected by the Word, so he is not treating his own reading as the Word. What binds him is the Word itself, and his conscience is where he answers to God for how faithfully he reads it. That is why no council can do it for him: an obligation cannot be handed to someone else.
Why it binds · the priesthood of all believers

“…whoever comes out of the water of baptism can boast that he is already a consecrated priest, bishop, and pope, although of course it is not seemly that just anybody should exercise such office.”

No one can stand before God in your place.
So no one can read the Word in your place.
Martin Luther, To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, 1520 · Luther’s Works 44
• One click. Why conscience is an obligation and not a preference. A year before Worms: “we are all consecrated priests through baptism, as St. Peter says in I Peter 2[:9].” Every baptized Christian has the Spirit within, is united with Christ, and stands before God directly.
• Older translation (C. M. Jacobs, 1915): “For whoever comes out of the water of baptism can boast that he is already consecrated priest, bishop and pope, though it is not seemly that every one should exercise the office.”

Luther did not invent this.
It was always true.

A council can make you say it. It cannot make you believe it.
One click. Point back at the egg: every council on it found this out. Nicaea named the Arians; it did not convert them. The settlement of 1662 ejected two thousand ministers; it did not persuade them. Luther only said out loud what had been true since the first council. Campbell, on a General Council: “It is not the voice of the multitude, but the voice of truth, that has power with the conscience”; “a conscience that awaits the decision of the multitude, that hangs in suspense for the casting vote of the majority, is a fit subject for the man of sin.”

So unity cannot be compelled.

You can compel conformity.
You cannot compel communion.
Two clicks. Why: the unity of the church is not everyone saying the same words. It is a communion of believers, each standing before God and joined to the others in Christ. Compel the words and you get conformity: the same sentence in divided hearts, which comes apart the moment a conscience stands up. That is the egg, every time.
August Noack, Religionsgespräch zu Marburg 1529 (detail), 1867–69 · public domain
Marburg · October 1529

Luther and Zwingli.

He could not share the Lord’s table with a brother who read the Lord’s table differently.
The painting (detail): Luther, left in the fur collar, holds Zwingli off with both hands; Zwingli points upward. In the full canvas Luther’s other hand is on the word est chalked on the table (“this is my body”). Fourteen articles agreed, and on the fifteenth agreement on everything but the bodily presence. Luther to the Swiss: “You have a different spirit.” As the accounts have it, Zwingli offered his hand at the end and Luther would not take it as a brother’s.
→ Two men, both captive to the same Word, reading it as faithfully as they could. Only one of them would grant the other that.

Luther claimed conscience for himself.
Campbell claimed it for his brother.

Say it once and stop. Not a new principle: the same principle, extended to the brother. Luther is not the villain here: the man of Worms and the man of Marburg were equally sincere. That is the point: conscience claimed for yourself is only half a sentence, and Campbell finishes it. This is the chapter in one line.
Preamble

“…as no man can be judged for his brother, so no man can judge for his brother; every man must be allowed to judge for himself, as every man must bear his own judgment—must give account of himself to God.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The Preamble’s second sentence: the half Luther could not say at Marburg. Not a right claimed but an impossibility stated: you cannot believe for someone else. Zurich and 1806 on the egg were the magistrate trying. The first sentence, just before it: “it is high time for us not only to think, but also to act, for ourselves… to this alone we feel ourselves Divinely bound to be conformed, as by this alone, we must be judged.”

The Declaration and Address
“my conscience is captive to the Word of God”
“to this alone we feel ourselves Divinely bound”
“I do not trust either in the pope or in councils alone”
“not the voice of the multitude, but the voice of truth”
“unless I am convinced by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason”
“not formally binding… farther than they perceive the connection”
“neither safe nor right to go against conscience”
“no man can judge for his brother”
Eight clicks, left then right on each row. Every line on the right is already on the left. The right column: the Preamble; the Address on a General Council; proposition 6; the Preamble again. Only the last row moves: Luther says I may not go against my conscience; Campbell says no one may go against his brother’s.
That last row is exactly where Luther stopped. Marburg, October 1529 (the 1529 slide on the egg): fourteen articles agreed, and on the fifteenth agreement on everything but the bodily presence. Luther to the Swiss: “Ihr habt einen andern Geist” — “You have a different spirit.” As the accounts have it, Zwingli offered his hand at the end and Luther would not take it as a brother’s.

The Campbells are not the precedent.
Luther is.

They took Worms more seriously than Luther’s heirs did,
and more seriously than Luther did, at Marburg.
Two clicks. Make it emphatic: nothing the Declaration says about conscience is new. The whole picture is in one sentence at Worms; Campbell is drawing out what it implies. Luther’s heirs: the Formula of Concord (1577) settled the Lutheran quarrels by drawing the line against the Reformed, and confessional Lutheran churches have kept a closed table since. Luther himself: Marburg, “You have a different spirit,” the hand not taken. If conscience is an obligation to the Word, Zwingli was under the same obligation, reading the same Word as faithfully as he could. Luther claimed conscience for himself and would not grant it to his brother.
→ So the one difference fits in a sentence.

If my brother is as bound to the Word as I am,

my reading cannot be his door to the table.
The table has to be open.
Two clicks. Three things in one line: freedom of conscience, why unity cannot be compelled, and the open table. This is Chapter 2 from the inside: Campbell was tried for opening the table to Presbyterians who read differently. Proposition 6 will make it rule: inferences are “not formally binding upon the consciences of Christians farther than they perceive the connection.” The Preamble’s word for the opposite: to judge your brother is “a daring usurpation of his throne, and a gross intrusion upon the rights and liberties of his subjects.”

What can Christians unite on?

“That they all may be one… that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.”
John 17:21
The question, now that the reason is named. Then the prayer: a prayer, not a command, and for the sake of the world’s belief. Pause on it before the answer.
Preamble, continued

“…nor, indeed, can we reasonably expect to find it anywhere but in Christ and his simple word, which is the same yesterday, to-day, and forever.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The clause you stopped before. Now it has fifteen hundred years behind it.
• → Thomas Campbell saw only one answer: given a people called to follow their conscience, given that no council could forever bind it, the only thing Christians could unite on was Christ himself.

There is nothing wrong with a creed.

But a creed cannot make us one.
Only Christ can do that.
Two clicks. Not anti-creed: Nicaea is true, and the room says it. The fault on the egg was never the creed; it was the job the creed was given.
Proposition 7

“…doctrinal exhibitions of the great system of Divine truths… be highly expedient, and the more full and explicit they be for those purposes, the better; yet… they ought not to be made terms of Christian communion…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Campbell says it himself: write the fullest confession you can. Just do not make it the door. Elided: “and defensive testimonies in opposition to prevailing errors”; “as these must be in a great measure the effect of human reasoning, and of course must contain many inferential truths.”
• The sentence ends: “the Church from the beginning did, and ever will, consist of little children and young men, as well as fathers.”

Every time we hand a creed, a council, or a magistrate
a job only Christ can do, it fails.

The chapter’s thesis. Point back at the egg: every one of those was a good instrument given the wrong job. Campbell names the job in the Address: creeds were “designed and embraced for the purpose of promoting and securing that desirable unity and purity which the Bible alone, without those helps, would be insufficient to maintain and secure.” That is the job description, and no document can do it.
→ So what does make us one?
The Address

“…the first and foundation truth of our Christianity is union with him, and the very next to it in order, union with each other in him.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Same sentence, just before: the “bewildered Church has, for hundreds of years past, been rending and dividing herself into factions, for Christ’s sake, and for the truth’s sake.” That is the egg in his words.
• Order matters: union with each other is not built beside union with Christ; it follows from it. That is proposition 1 in a sentence: given, not constructed.
Preamble, continued

“…taking the Divine word alone for our rule; the Holy Spirit for our teacher and guide, to lead us into all truth; and Christ alone, as exhibited in the word, for our salvation…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Guard: it is not creedless. “Christ alone, as exhibited in the word.” The fence is what Scripture expressly says, and nothing else. The propositions say how.
The Address

The Thirteen Propositions

Five of them.
Offered, the Address says just before them, not “as an overture toward a new creed or standard for the Church, or as in any wise designed to be made a term of communion.” Remember Chalcedon said the same. Read 1, 3, 6, 8, 9; the gold clause is the one to say twice.
Proposition 1

“That the Church of Christ upon earth is essentially, intentionally, and constitutionally one; consisting of all those in every place that profess their faith in Christ and obedience to him in all things according to the Scriptures, and that manifest the same by their tempers and conduct, and of none else…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The class has heard the opening clause twice; now the whole sentence. Stand two: do you believe unity is given rather than built? If so, the sects are the innovation.
Proposition 3

“That in order to do this, nothing ought to be inculcated upon Christians as articles of faith; nor required of them as terms of communion, but what is expressly taught and enjoined upon them in the word of God…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The method. “Expressly.” This is the whole wager: strip terms of communion to what Scripture expressly says, and Christians will find they already agree on enough to live together.
Proposition 6

“That although inferences and deductions from Scripture premises, when fairly inferred, may be truly called the doctrine of God’s holy word, yet are they not formally binding upon the consciences of Christians farther than they perceive the connection… Therefore, no such deductions can be made terms of communion…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Conscience again, now as polity. You cannot believe what you do not see, so you cannot be made to. Every council on the egg was an inference made a term of communion.
Proposition 8

“That as it is not necessary that persons should have a particular knowledge or distinct apprehension of all Divinely revealed truths in order to entitle them to a place in the Church; neither should they, for this purpose, be required to make a profession more extensive than their knowledge…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The one that answers Chalcedon directly: no term that excludes those who cannot understand it. The rest of the sentence: “a profession of their faith in and obedience to him, in all things, according to his word, is all that is absolutely necessary to qualify them for admission into his Church.”
Proposition 9

“That all that are enabled through grace to make such a profession… should consider each other as the precious saints of God, should love each other as brethren, children of the same family and Father, temples of the same Spirit, members of the same body… Whom God hath thus joined together no man should dare to put asunder.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The marriage line. Stand four: who are we not treating as brethren, and on what term?
Our table

What do we require of someone before they sit at our table?

“…a profession more extensive than their knowledge.”
Discussion, eight minutes. Have them list what we actually require. Then proposition 8 against the list: which of these is a profession more extensive than their knowledge? Every room has its Munro item; ours is not infant baptism. Leave it open. Set it against the Evils list: division already costs that; what would unity cost?
Resolution IV

“That this Society by no means considers itself a Church, nor does at all assume to itself the powers peculiar to such a society… but merely as voluntary advocates for Church reformation…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The one resolution to keep: voluntary advocates for reform, not a new church.
The reception
October 1810 · the Synod of Pittsburgh refuses Christian and ministerial communion. Nobody joins.
• Candor beat, one click. A unity plea addressed to every party and joined, in the event, by almost no one; the synod’s refusal is Week 5’s opening.
• → And the movement it started? We know what happened next.
The Churches of Christ

We have kept dividing.

We have all lived it.
Does that mean Thomas Campbell was wrong?
Two clicks. Let the first one sit: everyone in the room has a story of a split, a congregation, a family. Look back at the tree: one cup, non-class, non-institutional, instrumental, premillennial. Then ask the question and let them answer before the next slide.

No. It means he was right.

Every division since has come from someone
offering another answer than Christ.
There is no other answer. There never will be.
Two clicks. Campbell diagnosed the problem correctly; the divisions are what it looks like when his point is not taken as deeply as it merits. Cups, classes, institutions, instruments, the millennium: every one was made a term of communion, asked to do the job only Christ can do. It did what every instrument on the egg did.

Make anything else a term of communion,
and it will not make us one.
It will divide us again.

The thesis card, brought home: the egg was not only their history. It is ours. Proposition 3 was the remedy: nothing required as terms of communion “but what is expressly taught and enjoined upon them in the word of God.”
October 1809

Alexander, twenty-one, three weeks off the ship, reads the proof-sheets as they come from the printer.

Two sentences of Glasgow: the family wrecked off Islay, ten months in Glasgow, and the son refusing the Seceder communion token on his own, an ocean away from his father’s break. On the road from Philadelphia they find out they have each broken with the same fence, through the same table. Then the proof-sheets.
The warning

“Sir… these words, however plausible in appearance, are not sound. For if you follow these out, you must become a Baptist.”

Rev. Riddle, a neighboring Presbyterian minister, to Alexander · Richardson, Memoirs 1:251
• Alexander presses the question on his father: will these principles not mean giving up infant baptism? He buys every pro-infant-baptism treatise in Andrew Munro’s own bookshop to find out.
The answer

“We make our appeal to the law and to the testimony. Whatever is not found therein we must of course abandon.”

Thomas Campbell to his son, every time · Richardson 1:252
• The father’s answer committed the next generation before anyone knew where it led. Within three years the logic runs its course; that is a later week.

Next week: the rise and fall of the Springfield Presbytery.

Five years before this was printed, the men of Cane Ridge had already tried to live it.
Close. They built something, watched it succeed, and then did something almost without precedent in church history: they wrote a will for it. Chapter 4, October 18.
